Trigger: When finalizing a no-options yes/no imaging question asking whether the organs shown exist in the abdomen, and the rationale identifies the image as a chest X-ray with the main findings/organs being lungs and heart in the thorax.

Observable verification action: Re-read the earlier supported conclusion and the terminal answer together. If the main organs cited are thoracic—lungs and heart—choose “No” and keep the reason aligned: the main organs are thoracic, not abdominal. Because the option map is empty, do not invent a letter mapping; compare only the answer text with the released reference (“No” vs. “No”). If a structure such as the gastric bubble is partially visible at the bottom of the chest image, do not let that incidental finding flip the answer unless the question specifically asks about that structure. If tool observations are present, confirm they address the same image object and attribute as the question and that the terminal choice used them; here the observation log is empty, so the valid check is rationale-to-answer and answer-to-reference consistency, not image-evidence support. A correct grade alone does not prove the evidence procedure worked.

Trigger: Finalizing a comparative organ-abnormality answer such as “Which organ is abnormal, heart or lung?” when the terminal rationale cites a grounded imaging report.

Observable verification action: Locate the raw grounded-report statement for each candidate organ. Choose the organ only if its statement contains an explicit abnormal finding (for example, “mildly prominent cardiac silhouette” or “cardiomegaly”) and the other organ’s statement is explicitly negative or normal (for example, “lungs are free of infiltrates and masses”). Do not infer a heart abnormality from a normal-lung statement alone. If the raw tool observation containing the cited report phrase is absent from the transcript, do not treat the correct final grade as proof of the evidence procedure; retrieve or rerun the grounded report/verify step first. If options are displayed, map the supported organ text back to the displayed choice and confirm the letter and text agree. In this case no options were present, so the relevant check is evidence attribution: the answer “heart” is supported only if the grounded report actually names the cardiac abnormality while clearing the lungs.

Trigger: When finalizing a binary organ-abnormality answer such as “heart or lung” and the rationale cites specific imaging findings but the tool-observation log is empty.

Observable verification action: Parse the terminal organ label and compare it with the exact abnormal finding named in the answer’s reason. In this case, “lung” is consistent with the cited bilateral interstitial infiltrates and effusions, while the heart is described as upper-limit normal, so the selected organ and rationale agree. Because the options map is empty, do not invent a letter mapping; compare only the answer text with the released reference (“lung” vs. “Lung”). Also check the source of the cited findings: here there are no actual tool observations, so this verifies rationale-internal consistency and answer/reference agreement only, not image-evidence support. If tool observations are present, require that the named lung or heart finding came from an observation addressing that same organ and attribute, and that no conflicting observation was ignored.
